claim: Smc–ScpAB forms elongated, annular structures that promote chromosome segregation.
source: Smc–ScpAB forms elongated, annular structures that promote chromosome segregation, presumably by compacting and resolving sister DNA molecules.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general characterization of Smc-ScpAB function.

claim: Exclusively species of Smc–ScpA, which were previously cross-linked into covalent rings, remained associated with chromosomal DNA under protein denaturing conditions.
source: Exclusively species of Smc–ScpA, which were previously cross-linked into covalent rings, remained associated with chromosomal DNA.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the chromosome entrapment assay described in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 2.

claim: DNA entrapment is abolished by mutations that interfere with the Smc ATPase cycle.
source: DNA entrapment is abolished by mutations that interfere with the Smc ATPase cycle and strongly reduced when the recruitment factor ParB is deleted, implying that most Smc–ScpAB is loaded onto the chromosome at parS sites near the replication origin.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments with ATPase mutants shown in Figure 3.

claim: DNA entrapment is strongly reduced when the recruitment factor ParB is deleted.
source: DNA entrapment is abolished by mutations that interfere with the Smc ATPase cycle and strongly reduced when the recruitment factor ParB is deleted, implying that most Smc–ScpAB is loaded onto the chromosome at parS sites near the replication origin.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments with parB deletion shown in Figure 4.

claim: Most Smc–ScpAB is loaded onto the chromosome at parS sites near the replication origin.
source: DNA entrapment is abolished by mutations that interfere with the Smc ATPase cycle and strongly reduced when the recruitment factor ParB is deleted, implying that most Smc–ScpAB is loaded onto the chromosome at parS sites near the replication origin.
evidence: This is inferred from the strong reduction in DNA entrapment when ParB is deleted.

claim: There is a physical interaction between native Smc–ScpAB and chromosomal DNA fragments.
source: We furthermore report a physical interaction between native Smc–ScpAB and chromosomal DNA fragments.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-purification experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Condensin subunits were initially identified as abundant, non-histone components of mitotic chromosomes in metazoans.
source: Condensin subunits were initially identified as abundant, non-histone components of mitotic chromosomes in metazoans (Hirano and Mitchison, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hirano and Mitchison, 1994.

claim: In mitosis, condensin localizes together with topoisomerase II in punctate structures to the longitudinal core of chromatids, called the chromosome axis.
source: In mitosis, condensin localizes together with topoisomerase II in punctate structures to the longitudinal core of chromatids, called the chromosome axis (Coelho et al., 2003; Maeshima and Laemmli, 2003; Ono et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Coelho et al., 2003; Maeshima and Laemmli, 2003; Ono et al., 2004.

claim: Inactivation of condensin subunits by mutation or depletion results in severe morphological aberrations and mechanical sensitivity of metaphase chromosomes.
source: Inactivation of condensin subunits by mutation or depletion results in severe morphological aberrations and mechanical sensitivity of metaphase chromosomes, and subsequently to defects in their segregation during anaphase (Hirano and Mitchison, 1994; Ono et al., 2003; Gerlich et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hirano and Mitchison, 1994; Ono et al., 2003; Gerlich et al., 2006.

claim: In Bacillus subtilis and Streptococcus pneumoniae, Smc–ScpAB is recruited to a region around the replication origin by ParB/Spo0J protein bound to parS sites.
source: In Bacillus subtilis and Streptococcus pneumoniae, Smc–ScpAB is recruited to a region around the replication origin by ParB/Spo0J protein bound to parS sites, thereby forming a discrete focus—also called condensation center—on each nascent copy of the chromosome (Gruber and Errington, 2009; Sullivan et al., 2009; Minnen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gruber and Errington, 2009; Sullivan et al., 2009; Minnen et al., 2011.

claim: Inactivation of Smc–ScpAB in B. subtilis under nutrient rich growth conditions blocks separation of sister replication origins and leads to lethal defects in chromosome partitioning.
source: Inactivation of Smc–ScpAB in B. subtilis under nutrient rich growth conditions blocks separation of sister replication origins and consequentially leads to lethal defects in chromosome partitioning (Gruber et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gruber et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014.

claim: The canonical SMC complex in bacteria comprises five subunits: two Smc proteins, a single ScpA subunit, and a dimer of ScpB protein.
source: The canonical SMC complex in bacteria comprises five subunits: (1) two Smc proteins, which each form a 45 nm long antiparallel coiled coil that connects an ABC-type ATPase 'head' domain at one end of the coiled coil with a 'hinge' homodimerization domain at the other end (Hirano et al., 2001), (2) a single ScpA subunit, which belongs to the kleisin family of proteins and associates via its C-terminal winged-helix domain (WHD) with the bottom 'cap' surface of one Smc head and via its N-terminal helical domain with the 'neck' coiled coil region of the other Smc protein (Bürmann et al., 2013), and (3) a dimer of ScpB protein, which binds to the central region of ScpA (Bürmann et al., 2013; Kamada et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hirano et al., 2001; Bürmann et al., 2013; Kamada et al., 2013.

claim: The pentameric Smc–ScpAB complex displays a highly extended conformation harboring a central channel, which is surrounded by a closed tripartite ring.
source: Overall, the pentameric Smc–ScpAB complex displays a highly extended conformation harboring a central channel, which is surrounded by a closed tripartite ring formed by the Smc dimer and the ScpAB2 sub-complex.
evidence: This is a structural description based on previous work.

claim: The B. subtilis Smc coiled coils associate with one another to form rod-shaped Smc dimers.
source: The B. subtilis Smc coiled coils associate with one another to form rod-shaped Smc dimers (Soh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Soh et al., 2015.

claim: Non-crosslinkable DnaN-HT was efficiently depleted from agarose plugs during the entrapment assay.
source: Non-crosslinkable DnaN-HT was efficiently depleted from agarose plugs during the entrapment assay (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1C showing that non-crosslinked DnaN is removed during the assay.

claim: The double cross-linked, circular form of DnaN(N114C, V313C)-HT was retained in the agarose plug during electrophoresis with high efficiency (∼50% of input).
source: In contrast, the double cross-linked, circular form of DnaN(N114C, V313C)-HT (XX-DnaN-HT) was retained in the agarose plug during electrophoresis with high efficiency (∼50% of input).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1C showing retention of cross-linked DnaN in the agarose plug.

claim: The presence of benzonase during cell lysis eliminated all DnaN from the plug.
source: Importantly, the presence of benzonase during cell lysis eliminated all DnaN from the plug, indicating that circular DnaN is retained in plugs via its interaction with cellular DNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1C showing that nuclease treatment removes DnaN from plugs.

claim: Circular DnaN is retained in plugs via its interaction with cellular DNA.
source: Importantly, the presence of benzonase during cell lysis eliminated all DnaN from the plug, indicating that circular DnaN is retained in plugs via its interaction with cellular DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nuclease treatment releases DnaN from plugs.

claim: At least 50% of DnaN is loaded onto DNA in rapidly growing cells.
source: The chromosome entrapment assay thus specifically detects a topological association of intact chromosomes with DNA sliding clamps and confirms that a major fraction (at least 50%) of DnaN is loaded onto DNA in rapidly growing cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the ~50% retention of cross-linked DnaN in the entrapment assay.

claim: Strains bearing the cysteine mutations and the Smc-HaloTag fusion supported normal growth on nutrient rich medium.
source: Strains bearing the cysteine mutations and the Smc-HaloTag fusion supported normal growth on nutrient rich medium demonstrating the functionality of the modified Smc complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A showing colony formation assays.

claim: In control samples lacking all pairs of cysteine, little or no Smc-HT protein was retained in agarose plugs under denaturing conditions.
source: In these control samples little or no Smc-HT protein was retained in agarose plugs under denaturing conditions as expected for any non-circular protein (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B showing that non-circular Smc is not retained.

claim: In the presence of all pairs of cysteine, a set of two closely migrating species was consistently detected at significant levels after the chromosome entrapment assay (∼10–20% of input material).
source: In the presence of all pairs of cysteine, however, a set of two closely migrating species was consistently detected at significant levels after the chromosome entrapment assay (∼10–20% of input material) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B showing retention of cross-linked Smc species.

claim: Incubation of agarose plugs with the nuclease benzonase during cell lysis eliminated the Smc-HT and DnaN signal in the sample.
source: Incubation of agarose plugs with the nuclease benzonase during cell lysis eliminated the Smc-HT and DnaN signal in the sample (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B showing that nuclease treatment removes Smc from plugs.

claim: Little or no Smc-HT signal was detected in agarose plugs after TEV cleavage of ScpA.
source: As expected, little or no Smc-HT signal was detected in agarose plugs after TEV cleavage of ScpA (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2D showing that opening the ring prevents retention.

claim: The chromosome entrapment assay specifically detects the association between intact chromosomal DNA and rings of Smc–ScpAB in B. subtilis.
source: Thus, our chromosome entrapment assay specifically detects the association between intact chromosomal DNA and rings of Smc–ScpAB in B. subtilis, demonstrating that DNA fibers pass through the Smc ring.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined results of cross-linking, nuclease treatment, and TEV cleavage experiments.

claim: DNA fibers pass through the Smc ring.
source: Thus, our chromosome entrapment assay specifically detects the association between intact chromosomal DNA and rings of Smc–ScpAB in B. subtilis, demonstrating that DNA fibers pass through the Smc ring.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for intact rings and DNA for retention in the assay.

claim: The three mutant Smc proteins (K37I, S1090R, E1118Q) are expressed at normal levels in B. subtilis.
source: The three mutant proteins are expressed at normal levels in B. subtilis being indicative of proper protein folding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A showing Western blot analysis.

claim: The three Smc ATPase mutants (K37I, S1090R, E1118Q) do not support growth on nutrient rich medium similar to smc null mutants.
source: However, they do not support growth on nutrient rich medium similar to smc null mutants, implying that all steps of the ATPase cycle are essential for Smc functionality (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) (Gruber et al., 2014).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B showing colony formation assays.

claim: All steps of the ATPase cycle are essential for Smc functionality.
source: However, they do not support growth on nutrient rich medium similar to smc null mutants, implying that all steps of the ATPase cycle are essential for Smc functionality (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) (Gruber et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all ATPase mutants fail to support growth.

claim: The ATP binding and engagement mutants abolished the fraction of covalent ring species retained in the agarose plug during the chromosome entrapment assay.
source: Intriguingly, the ATP binding and engagement mutants abolished the fraction of covalent ring species retained in the agarose plug during the chromosome entrapment assay (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3B showing that K37I and S1090R mutants do not retain Smc in plugs.

claim: In case of the ATP hydrolysis mutant Smc(E1118Q) only minute amounts of cross-linked rings were recovered from SDS treated plugs.
source: In case of the ATP hydrolysis mutant Smc(E1118Q) only minute amounts of cross-linked rings were recovered from SDS treated plugs.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3B showing reduced retention of E1118Q mutant.

claim: ATP binding and ATP dependent Smc head engagement—and most probably also ATP hydrolysis—are essential for entrapment of chromosomal DNA by condensin in bacteria.
source: Thus, ATP binding and ATP dependent Smc head engagement—and most probably also ATP hydrolysis—are essential for entrapment of chromosomal DNA by condensin in bacteria, as has been supposed for cohesin in yeast.
evidence: This is concluded from the results with ATPase mutants in the entrapment assay.

claim: Smc complexes lacking ScpB subunits failed to entrap chromosomes.
source: However, Smc complexes lacking ScpB subunits failed to entrap chromosomes altogether demonstrating that ScpB is absolutely required for loading of prokaryotic condensin onto chromosomal DNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4A showing no retention of Smc in ΔscpB mutant.

claim: ScpB is absolutely required for loading of prokaryotic condensin onto chromosomal DNA.
source: However, Smc complexes lacking ScpB subunits failed to entrap chromosomes altogether demonstrating that ScpB is absolutely required for loading of prokaryotic condensin onto chromosomal DNA.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that ΔscpB abolishes DNA entrapment.

claim: The levels of Smc–ScpAB entrapping chromosomal DNA were strongly reduced in the parB null mutant.
source: Intriguingly, the levels of Smc–ScpAB entrapping chromosomal DNA were strongly reduced in the parB null mutant as judged by the limited retention of Smc–ScpA species in agarose plugs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4B showing reduced retention of Smc in ΔparB mutant.

claim: ParB protein likely promotes the entrapment of chromosomal DNA by Smc–ScpAB.
source: Thus, ParB protein likely promotes the entrapment of chromosomal DNA by Smc–ScpAB.
evidence: This is inferred from the strong reduction in DNA entrapment when ParB is deleted.

claim: Most condensin is loaded onto the chromosome at parS sites, where ParB protein is bound.
source: This strongly suggests that most condensin is loaded onto the chromosome at parS sites, where ParB protein is bound.
evidence: This is inferred from the strong reduction in DNA entrapment when ParB is deleted.

claim: Two parB point mutations (N112S and R149G) strongly impair loading of Smc onto the chromosome in the entrapment assay similar to ΔparB.
source: We found that these mutations strongly impair loading of Smc onto the chromosome in the entrapment assay similar to ΔparB (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4B showing reduced retention of Smc with parB point mutants.

claim: ParB mutants G77S and R80A resulted in largely reduced levels of Smc on the chromosome in the entrapment assay, comparable to the levels found in a parB deletion mutant.
source: Intriguingly, also these mutations resulted in largely reduced levels of Smc on the chromosome in our entrapment assay, being comparable to the levels found in a parB deletion mutant (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4B showing reduced retention of Smc with G77S and R80A mutants.

claim: ParB spreading from parS sites or formation of large nucleoprotein complexes might be essential for loading of DNA into the Smc ring by ParB.
source: This implies that ParB spreading from parS sites or formation of large nucleoprotein complexes might be essential for loading of DNA into the Smc ring by ParB.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that spreading-defective ParB mutants fail to promote Smc loading.

claim: A small fraction of chromosomal DNA was reproducibly co-purified with wild-type Smc-Avitag.
source: A small fraction of chromosomal DNA was reproducibly co-purified with wild-type Smc-Avitag, whereas the yield of co-purified DNA was significantly improved by the presence of cross-linkable cysteine residues in Smc–ScpAB (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5 showing co-purification of DNA with Smc.

claim: The yield of co-purified DNA was significantly improved by the presence of cross-linkable cysteine residues in Smc–ScpAB.
source: A small fraction of chromosomal DNA was reproducibly co-purified with wild-type Smc-Avitag, whereas the yield of co-purified DNA was significantly improved by the presence of cross-linkable cysteine residues in Smc–ScpAB (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5 showing increased DNA co-purification with cross-linked Smc.

claim: Origin-proximal regions of the chromosome were more efficiently enriched than distal regions by the co-purification with Smc.
source: In both cases origin-proximal regions (yyaD, parS-359, dnaA and dnaN) of the chromosome were more efficiently enriched than distal regions (amyE, trnS and ter) by the co-purification with Smc implying that the observed Smc-DNA contacts are dependent on chromosomal loading of Smc–ScpAB by ParB protein at parS sites and are thus physiologically relevant (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) (Gruber and Errington, 2009).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5 showing preferential enrichment of origin-proximal DNA.

claim: The observed Smc-DNA contacts are dependent on chromosomal loading of Smc–ScpAB by ParB protein at parS sites and are thus physiologically relevant.
source: In both cases origin-proximal regions (yyaD, parS-359, dnaA and dnaN) of the chromosome were more efficiently enriched than distal regions (amyE, trnS and ter) by the co-purification with Smc implying that the observed Smc-DNA contacts are dependent on chromosomal loading of Smc–ScpAB by ParB protein at parS sites and are thus physiologically relevant (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) (Gruber and Errington, 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the preferential enrichment of origin-proximal DNA.

claim: The association of DNA with wild-type and BMOE cross-linked Smc–ScpAB was highly sensitive to washes with a salt solution (2M NaCl).
source: The association of DNA with wild-type and BMOE cross-linked Smc–ScpAB was highly sensitive to washes with a salt solution (2M NaCl), suggesting that it was dependent on electrostatic contacts between DNA and protein.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5 showing loss of DNA co-purification with high salt wash.

claim: The association of DNA with Smc–ScpAB was dependent on electrostatic contacts between DNA and protein.
source: The association of DNA with wild-type and BMOE cross-linked Smc–ScpAB was highly sensitive to washes with a salt solution (2M NaCl), suggesting that it was dependent on electrostatic contacts between DNA and protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the salt sensitivity of the DNA-protein interaction.

claim: Embracement of chromosomal DNA is a predominant feature of Smc–ScpAB, which has been evolutionarily retained in cohesin and likely all other SMC–kleisin complexes as well.
source: Our results show that embracement of chromosomal DNA is a predominant feature of Smc–ScpAB, which has been evolutionarily retained in cohesin and likely all other SMC–kleisin complexes as well.
evidence: This is concluded from the DNA entrapment results and evolutionary conservation of SMC complexes.

claim: A recent single-molecule tracking study in B. subtilis revealed two major populations of Smc: 80% of Smc-YFP proteins are displaying highly dynamic behavior on the nucleoid, whereas the other 20% (and most ScpA-YFP protein) are immobile and constrained within a small volume of the cell.
source: Interestingly, a recent single-molecule tracking study in B. subtilis revealed two major populations of Smc: 80% of Smc-YFP proteins are displaying highly dynamic behavior on the nucleoid, whereas the other 20% (and most ScpA-YFP protein) are immobile and constrained within a small volume of the cell (Kleine Borgmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kleine Borgmann et al., 2013.

claim: The immobile fraction of Smc possibly represents Smc–ScpAB complexes embracing origin proximal DNA after loading at parS sites.
source: This immobile fraction possibly represents Smc–ScpAB complexes embracing origin proximal DNA after loading at parS sites as observed in the entrapment assay.
evidence: This is speculated based on the correlation between the immobile fraction and the fraction retained in the entrapment assay.

claim: The average number of Smc protein is around 30 dimers per replication origin in a fast growing population of cells.
source: Using quantitative blotting of Smc protein and replication origin DNA from cell extracts, we have estimated the average number of Smc protein to be around 30 dimers per replication origin in a fast growing population of cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing quantitative Western and Southern blotting.

claim: Only three to six Smc dimers (10–20% of total) are loaded onto the chromosome in parB mutants.
source: Assuming that all Smc complexes entrap chromosomal DNA in wild-type cells, only three to six Smc dimers (10–20% of total) are loaded onto the chromosome in parB mutants according to our measurements.
evidence: This is calculated from the estimated total Smc and the fraction retained in parB mutants.

claim: A handful of Smc–ScpAB complexes, which are presumably randomly distributed over the chromosome, appears to be capable of supporting near-normal chromosome segregation under these conditions.
source: Thus, a handful of Smc–ScpAB complexes, which are presumably randomly distributed over the chromosome, appears to be capable of supporting near-normal chromosome segregation under these conditions—when chromosome segregation is already compromised by the loss of the parABS system.
evidence: This is inferred from the mild segregation defects in parB mutants despite low Smc loading.

claim: Individual Smc–ScpAB complexes are able to organize large chunks of a bacterial chromosome, possible by forming giant loops of DNA.
source: It is conceivable that individual Smc–ScpAB complexes are able to organize large chunks of a bacterial chromosome, possible by forming giant loops of DNA.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that few Smc complexes can support chromosome segregation.

claim: When levels of functional Smc dimers are in addition reduced for example by hypomorphic mutations in the smc gene itself, the loss of ParB protein becomes lethal.
source: However, when levels of functional Smc dimers are in addition reduced for example by hypomorphic mutations in the smc gene itself, the loss of ParB protein becomes lethal (Gruber and Errington, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gruber and Errington, 2009.

claim: The structurally related cohesin complex holds sister chromatids in eukaryotes together by entrapping sister DNA fibers within its ring.
source: A different hypothesis is based on the finding that the structurally related cohesin complex holds sister chromatids in eukaryotes together by entrapping sister DNA fibers within its ring (Gruber et al., 2003; Gligoris et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gruber et al., 2003; Gligoris et al., 2014.

claim: Most of cellular DnaN protein is maintained in the vicinity of active replication forks in B. subtilis, presumably by its topological association with leading and lagging strand DNA.
source: Furthermore, most of cellular DnaN protein is maintained in the vicinity of active replication forks in B. subtilis, presumably by its topological association with leading and lagging strand DNA (Su'etsugu and Errington, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Su'etsugu and Errington, 2011.

claim: The dnaN-ht genes with and without cysteine mutations supported normal growth of B. subtilis.
source: The dnaN-ht genes with and without cysteine mutations supported normal growth of B. subtilis, implying that they encoded functional DnaN proteins (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from growth experiments.

claim: In the absence of the cross-linker BMOE, no DnaN-HT was detected in the eluate fraction.
source: Furthermore, in the absence of the cross-linker BMOE, no DnaN-HT was detected in the eluate fraction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C showing no retention without cross-linking.

claim: Ring formation was only mildly affected by the absence of ScpB as judged by BMOE cross-linking and in-gel fluorescence detection.
source: Ring formation was only mildly affected by the absence of ScpB as judged by BMOE cross-linking and in-gel fluorescence detection (Figure 4A) (Bürmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4A showing cross-linking patterns in ΔscpB.

claim: The R149G mutation is positioned on the helix-turn-helix motif of ParB and might thus directly affect binding to parS sites.
source: The R149G mutation is positioned on the helix-turn-helix motif of ParB and might thus directly affect binding to parS sites (Leonard et al., 2004).
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural location of the mutation and supported by a citation to Leonard et al., 2004.

claim: The N112S mutation is located in another highly conserved region, which has been implicated in the 'spreading' of ParB protein from parS sequences into adjacent DNA.
source: The N112S mutation, however, is located in another highly conserved region, which has been implicated in the 'spreading' of ParB protein from parS sequences into adjacent DNA (Leonard et al., 2004; Graham et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Leonard et al., 2004; Graham et al., 2014.

claim: The spreading of ParB along several kb of DNA is a feature conserved in plasmid and chromosome derived ParB proteins.
source: The spreading of ParB along several kb of DNA is a feature conserved in plasmid and chromosome derived ParB proteins, however, the underlying mechanism is only poorly understood (Rodionov et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rodionov et al., 1999.

claim: Several other mutants of ParB (including B. subtilis ParB G77S and R80A) have been reported to be defective in spreading from parS sites.
source: Several other mutants of ParB (including B. subtilis ParB G77S and R80A) have been reported to be defective in spreading from parS sites (Breier and Grossman, 2007; Graham et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Breier and Grossman, 2007; Graham et al., 2014.

claim: ParB spreading from parS sites or formation of large nucleoprotein complexes might be essential for loading of DNA into the Smc ring by ParB.
source: This implies that ParB spreading from parS sites or formation of large nucleoprotein complexes might be essential for loading of DNA into the Smc ring by ParB.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that spreading-defective mutants fail to promote Smc loading.

claim: Formation of Smc-GFP foci near the origin of replication are affected by the G77S mutation.
source: These findings are consistent with the observation that formation of Smc-GFP foci near the origin of replication are affected by the G77S mutation (Sullivan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sullivan et al., 2009.

claim: Smc proteins and fragments thereof exhibit affinity for single- and double-stranded DNA in vitro.
source: Smc proteins and fragments thereof exhibit affinity for single- and double-stranded DNA in vitro (Chiu et al., 2004; Hirano and Hirano, 2006; Soh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chiu et al., 2004; Hirano and Hirano, 2006; Soh et al., 2015.

claim: The intrinsic ATPase activity of cohesin has previously been implicated in stable association with chromosomes.
source: The intrinsic ATPase activity of cohesin has previously been implicated in stable association with chromosomes (Arumugam et al., 2003; Weitzer et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arumugam et al., 2003; Weitzer et al., 2003.

claim: ATP hydrolysis has been hypothesized to transiently open an entry gate for DNA in the cohesin ring during its loading onto chromosomes.
source: More specifically, ATP hydrolysis has been hypothesized to transiently open an entry gate for DNA in the cohesin ring during its loading onto chromosomes (Gruber et al., 2006; Hu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gruber et al., 2006; Hu et al., 2011.

claim: The three mutant Smc proteins assembled into normal Smc–ScpAB complexes as judged by Smc–ScpA cross-linking.
source: The three mutant Smc proteins assembled into normal Smc–ScpAB complexes as judged by Smc–ScpA cross-linking, albeit there is a slight decrease in the fraction of ScpA proteins bridging Smc dimers and a concomitant minor increase in ScpA subunits bound to single Smc proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, species 'e' and 'd', respectively) (Bürmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C showing cross-linking patterns of mutant Smc.

claim: There is a slight decrease in the fraction of ScpA proteins bridging Smc dimers and a concomitant minor increase in ScpA subunits bound to single Smc proteins in ATPase mutants.
source: The three mutant Smc proteins assembled into normal Smc–ScpAB complexes as judged by Smc–ScpA cross-linking, albeit there is a slight decrease in the fraction of ScpA proteins bridging Smc dimers and a concomitant minor increase in ScpA subunits bound to single Smc proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, species 'e' and 'd', respectively) (Bürmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C showing altered cross-linking patterns.

claim: The small fraction of stably bound condensin in the E1118Q mutant conceivably arises as a consequence of residual levels of ATP hydrolysis activity in Smc(E1118Q).
source: This small fraction of stably bound condensin conceivably arises as a consequence of residual levels of ATP hydrolysis activity in Smc(E1118Q) (Hirano and Hirano, 2004).
evidence: This is speculated based on known properties of the E1118Q mutation and supported by a citation to Hirano and Hirano, 2004.

claim: The strict requirement of several steps of the ATPase cycle strongly suggests that entrapment of DNA corresponds to the physiological form of association with the bacterial chromosome.
source: Furthermore, the strict requirement of several steps of the ATPase cycle strongly suggests that entrapment of DNA corresponds to the physiological form of association with the bacterial chromosome.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ATPase mutants abolish DNA entrapment.

claim: The cysteine bearing smc allele causes growth defects when combined with ΔparB.
source: The cysteine bearing smc allele causes growth defects when combined with ΔparB (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing colony formation assays.

claim: We cannot formally exclude the possibility that the decreased loading of Smc observed in ΔparB are due to the cysteine modifications in Smc and that chromosomal loading of wild-type Smc is not or much less affected by parB deletion.
source: Therefore, we cannot formally exclude the possibility that the decreased loading of Smc observed in ΔparB are due to the cysteine modifications in Smc and that chromosomal loading of wild-type Smc is not or much less affected by parB deletion.
evidence: This is a caveat acknowledged by the authors regarding the interpretation of the parB deletion results.
